X trained at the Royal Academy in London and won a gold medal in Britain for a painting of a dying Hercules. He painted portraits of Presidents John Adams and James Monroe, of the inventor Eli Whitney, and of the Marquis de Lafayette. X was also the first president of the National Academy of Design, serving from 1826 to 1845.
In 1825, while in Washington painting Lafayette's portrait, he received a letter by horse messenger informing him that his wife Lucretia was gravely ill. The next day, a second letter arrived saying she had died. By the time X reached home, she had already been buried.
In 1832, on a ship called the Sully returning from Europe, X fell into conversation with a passenger who demonstrated experiments with electromagnetism. X became so consumed by the possibilities that he abandoned the painting he had been working on, The Gallery of the Louvre. When X built the first working prototype of the device that would define his legacy, he used a painter's canvas stretcher as its frame. ID X.
